blocks.text: A coil is connected in series with a battery, a switch and a rheostat (Fig 17.18). If the rheostat is moved quickly, the current through the coil changes, so the magnetic flux through the coil changes, which induces an emf in the coil itself.

blocks.title: Self-induction
blocks.text: Self-induction is the phenomenon in which a changing current induces an emf in the coil itself.

Let phi be the flux through one loop of the coil; the flux through N turns is N phi. As phi is proportional to the magnetic field, which is proportional to the current I, N phi is proportional to I: N phi = LI (17.29), where the constant L is the self-inductance of the coil. L depends on the number of turns, the area of cross-section of the coil and the core material: winding the coil around a ferromagnetic iron core increases the flux, and so the inductance, greatly compared with an air core.

By Faraday's law the induced emf is eL = -N d(phi)/dt (17.30) = -d(N phi)/dt = -d(LI)/dt, so eL = -L dI/dt (17.31), or L = -eL / (dI/dt) (17.32). The minus sign shows that the induced emf opposes the change in current. Equating 17.30 and 17.31 also gives L = N d(phi)/dI (17.33).

blocks.title: The henry
blocks.text: A coil has a self-inductance of 1 henry (H) if an emf of 1 V is induced in it when the current through it changes at the rate of 1 A s^-1. The SI unit of self-inductance is V s A^-1 (the henry), with dimensions [M L^2 T^-2 A^-2].
A coil has an inductive reactance of 160 ohm at 50 Hz. Find its self-inductance. Solution: XL = 2 pi f L, so L = XL / (2 pi f) = 160 ohm / (2 x 3.14 x 50 Hz) = 0.509 H.

A coil is connected to a battery and a switch (Fig 17.19). When the switch is closed the current rises from zero to its final value I, and the changing current induces an emf opposing the battery; the battery must do work to move charge against it. The work to move a small charge dq is W = dq eL (17.34), with eL = L dI/dt, so W = dq L (dI/dt) = (dq/dt) L dI (17.35). Here dq/dt is the average current, (0 + I)/2 = I/2, and dI = I - 0 = I. So W = (I/2) L I = (1/2) L I^2 (17.36). This work is stored as potential energy in the magnetic field: Um = (1/2) L I^2 (17.37). It can never be negative, because it depends on the square of the current; the inductor absorbs energy while the current grows and returns it when the current falls.

blocks.alt: A coil connected to a battery through a switch; the current I flows up into one end of the coil and out of the other. Magnetic field lines spread out from both ends of the coil. A curved red arrow labelled induced current shows the induced current, which opposes the rise of I.
blocks.caption: Figure 17.19: Circuit designed to calculate energy stored in an inductor (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 17.19).

blocks.text: For a solenoid with n turns per unit length, cross-section A and length l, B = mu_o n I and L = mu_o n^2 A l. Substituting gives Um = (1/2) mu_o n^2 A l (B / mu_o n)^2 = (B^2 / 2 mu_o)(A l), where A l is the volume. So the energy density of the magnetic field is Um / volume = B^2 / (2 mu_o) (17.38).
